Lifecycle Hook — это функция, которую Strapi вызывает сам, до или после операции с записью. Создаёте статью — сначала срабатывает `beforeCreate`, потом запись уходит в базу, потом срабатывает `afterCreate`. Вызывать хук вручную не нужно: он привязан к Content Type и работает при любом обращении — из REST API, из админки, из вашего сервиса.

Нужны они там, где логика повторяется при каждой операции и не относится к конкретному месту вызова: сгенерировать slug, записать строку в аудит, сбросить кеш. В Prisma то же самое делает middleware, в Mongoose — pre/post hooks.

worst_places.after:
Strapi построен на Koa.js — минималистичном Node.js-фреймворке. «Минималистичный» здесь значит, что сам Koa умеет немного: принять HTTP-запрос и пропустить его через цепочку функций-обработчиков (middleware). Всё остальное добавляет Strapi.

Путь запроса такой: сначала общие middleware (разбор тела, CORS, аутентификация), потом router выбирает обработчик по URL, потом policy решает, есть ли у пользователя доступ, потом controller разбирает запрос, service выполняет бизнес-логику, Document Service читает и пишет данные, и в самом низу — база данных. Ниже каждый шаг разобран отдельно; если вы знаете NestJS, порядок ровно тот же.

worst_places.after:
## Policies, Middlewares and RBAC

## Two authorization spaces in Strapi

Strapi checks permissions in two completely separate systems, and mixing them up is the usual source of confusion. Both use RBAC — role-based access control, meaning a user gets a role and the role, not the user, carries the permissions. One system covers the people who use your app through the API; the other covers the editors who log into the Admin Panel. They share no roles, no tokens and no settings screen.

worst_places.before: Solutions: (1) Distributed lock via Redis — acquire a lock with TTL before executing the task, only one instance does the work; (2) move the Cron to a separate worker process/Lambda running as a single instance; (3) use BullMQ for a task queue with a single worker.
worst_places.after:
Three ways out:

1. **A distributed lock in Redis.** Before running the task, an instance takes a lock with a TTL (time to live — the lock expires by itself, so a crashed instance cannot block the job forever). Only the instance that got the lock does the work.
2. **Move the Cron out.** Run it in a separate worker process or a Lambda, started as a single instance.
3. **Use a queue.** BullMQ with one worker gives you the same guarantee plus retries.

patterns: The structural habit that defines this zone: **heading, then straight into a code block, with no sentence in between.** 24 of the 33 body sections across the seven articles do this. Measured, every file is 52-75% code by word count (ru/05: 629 of 848 words; ru/06: 666 of 890; en/02: 571 of 797). The consequence is that every concept in the topic is introduced by name inside a code comment or an ASCII table rather than defined in prose — Policy, Middleware, API Token, Dynamic Zone, Component, Bootstrap, Register, Cron Job, EventHub, Query Engine, sanitizeOutput. The reader is asked to infer the idea from a 50-line TypeScript listing on a phone. Nothing here needs cutting; each of those sections needs a 3-5 sentence lead added above the existing code.

**The teaching has migrated to the bottom of the file.** The «Типичные ошибки на интервью» / «Common interview mistakes» bullet list carries 64-96% of all non-code words in every article 01-06 (ru/05: 211 of 219 prose words = 96%; en/03: 228 of 252 = 90%; en/05: 240 of 250 = 96%). Those bullets are genuinely the best writing in the zone — «Policy и Middleware — одно и то же» — нет. Middleware выполняется раньше...» is exactly the plain-language definition the body needed. So the answer to the zone question is: it is not that 4.3k words are too few to teach anything, it is that the explanatory prose is all in the last screen of each file, and the body above it is a code dump. The material for the missing leads already exists inside the article — it just needs to be moved up.

**Every concept is anchored to another framework the reader may not know.** Content Type is «Аналог таблицы в БД + Prisma Model + NestJS Entity». Policy is «аналог Guard в NestJS». Lifecycle Hooks are «Аналог Prisma middleware или Mongoose pre/post hooks». Middleware is «аналог Koa/Express middleware». Two of the seven articles carry a full Strapi-vs-NestJS comparison table. This is a good habit turned into the only habit: an analogy is a shortcut for readers who have the reference, and nothing at all for readers who do not. Every one needs to follow a first-principles sentence, not replace it.

**Version drift inside single files.** Article 01 tells the reader v5 removed the nested `attributes` wrapper, and its own REST example above returns the v4 `data`/`attributes` shape; article 03's Dynamic Zone response does the same; article 05's is-admin policy calls `strapi.entityService.findOne` (the v4 API that articles 02, 04 and 07 all say was replaced). Articles are read out of order, so nothing tells a reader landing on 03 or 05 that the example they are copying is a major version behind. Every code block in this zone needs a version marker in its first comment line.
notes: B is the zone's best score (4.0 flat — 3 long sentences in 14 files, no bureaucratic register, no genitive chains). C at 1.3 and D at 1.4 are the worst two scores I would expect to see anywhere on this site, and they measure the same defect: not dense prose, but absent prose. Volume is not the problem the way the zone brief framed it — 4.3k words could teach this material; the issue is that ~70% of those words are inside code fences and ~90% of what remains is the closing pitfalls list, so the average article body is 10-30 words of explanation for 600 words of code. Fixing this zone means adding, not rewriting: a lead paragraph per section (~150 words x 33 sections), lifted largely from the pitfalls lists that already exist. EN and RU are near-identical translations of the same skeleton, so every finding above applies to both locales; EN is not harder than RU here (F 3.9) precisely because there is so little prose to be hard.
